Apply [L2] with $\Omega=Q$, $M\equiv m$, the potential $U$ and $q_{0}=x_{*}$: it produces $\delta>0$ such that every solution $(q,v)$ of the mechanical system with $\lVert(q(0),v(0))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert(q(t),v(t))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$. derivations.claim: **Unit-circle parametrisation.** For reals $c,s$ with $c^{2}+s^{2}=1$ there is a real $\theta$ with $\cos\theta=c$ and $\sin\theta=s$. Indeed, $c\in[-1,1]$ because $c^{2}\le c^{2}+s^{2}=1$; cosine is continuous on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos0=1$ and $\cos\pi=-1$, so by [L4] there is $\theta_{1}\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta_{1}=c$. Then $\sin^{2}\theta_{1}=1-c^{2}=s^{2}$ by [L3], and $\sin\theta_{1}\ge0$ on $[0,\pi]$ by [L3]; hence $\sin\theta_{1}=\lvert s\rvert$. If $s\ge0$ take $\theta=\theta_{1}$; if $s<0$ take $\theta=-\theta_{1}$, so that $\cos\theta=\cos\theta_{1}=c$ and $\sin\theta=-\sin\theta_{1}=\lvert s\rvert=s$ by the parity identities of [L3].

**The periods of cosine.** If $T$ is a real number with $\cos(u+T)=\cos u$ for all $u$, then $T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. Indeed, taking $u=\pi/2$ gives $\cos(\pi/2+T)=0$, so $\pi/2+T=(m+1/2)\pi$ for an integer $m$ by [L4], that is $T=m\pi$; taking $u=0$ gives $\cos T=1$. From $\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x$ and $\cos0=1$ of [L3], induction on $\lvert m\rvert$ gives $\cos(m\pi)=(-1)^{m}$ for every integer $m$; hence $(-1)^{m}=1$ and $m$ is even, so $T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. Conversely $T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ is a period of cosine by [L4].

Clause 1. Let $x:J\to\mathbb R$ be a motion and $t_{0}\in J$. The shifted curve $y(s):=x(t_{0}+s)$ is defined on the interval $J-t_{0}$ with nonempty interior and satisfies $m\,y''+k\,y=0$ there (the equation has no explicit time dependence). By [L2] there are $A,B$ with $y(s)=A\cos(\omega s)+B\sin(\omega s)$, that is $x(t)=A\cos(\omega(t-t_{0}))+B\sin(\omega(t-t_{0}))$ on $J$. Conversely each function of this form is obtained by shifting a solution of [L2] and is therefore a motion. For the datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ apply [L2] to $y$ with $y(0)=x_{0}$ and $y'(0)=v_{0}$: there is exactly one solution on $\mathbb R$, namely $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; translating back gives the unique maximal motion, defined on $\mathbb R$, and every motion with the datum is a restriction by the uniqueness in clause 1 of [[pthm-cm04-conservative-motion-and-energy]]. This is clause 1.

Clause 2. Write $\theta(t):=\omega(t-t_{0})$. For every real $\theta$, $$R^{2}-\bigl(A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta\bigr)^{2} =A^{2}\sin^{2}\theta+B^{2}\cos^{2}\theta-2AB\sin\theta\cos\theta =\bigl(A\sin\theta-B\cos\theta\bigr)^{2}\ge0,$$ where only the expansion of the squares and $\sin^{2}+\cos^{2}=1$ of [L3] were used; hence $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$. If $R>0$, apply step 1.1 to $(c,s)=(A/R,B/R)$, which satisfies $c^{2}+s^{2}=1$: there is $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and $\sin\varphi=B/R$. The addition formula of [L3] gives $$\cos\bigl(\theta-\varphi\bigr)=\cos\theta\cos\varphi+\sin\theta\sin\varphi=\frac{A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta}{R},$$ so $x(t)=R\cos(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi)$. If $R=0$ then $A=B=0$ and $x\equiv0$. This is clause 2.

Clause 4, the energy. With $\theta=\omega(t-t_{0})$ the derivative of $x$ is $x'(t)=\omega\bigl(-A\sin\theta+B\cos\theta\bigr)$ by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. Using $m\omega^{2}=k$ from [L1], $$E=\tfrac12m\,x'^{2}+\tfrac12k\,x^{2} =\tfrac12k\Bigl[\bigl(-A\sin\theta+B\cos\theta\bigr)^{2}+\bigl(A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta\bigr)^{2}\Bigr] =\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2},$$ expanding the squares and using $\sin^{2}+\cos^{2}=1$ of [L3]; in particular the energy is the constant $\tfrac12kR^{2}$, in agreement with the conservation clause of [L5]. This is the first assertion of clause 4.

Clause 3. If $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, then by [L4] the cosine is $2\pi$-periodic, so $\cos(\theta+\omega T)=\cos\theta$ and $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for all $t$; this covers the case $R=0$ as well. Suppose $R>0$ and $T>0$ is a period of $x$. Dividing clause 2 by $R$, $\cos(\omega(t+T-t_{0})-\varphi)=\cos(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi)$ for all $t$; as $t$ ranges over $\mathbb R$, $u:=\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi$ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$, so $\omega T$ is a period of cosine; by step 1.2, $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence the positive periods of a nonconstant harmonic motion are exactly the numbers $2\pi n/\omega$, $n\ge1$, and the least one is $2\pi/\omega$. This is clause 3.

Clause 4, the ellipse. Hence every point of $\Sigma_{R}$ lies on the phase curve, at the displayed times. If $R=0$ then $x\equiv0$ by clause 2 and the phase curve is $\{(0,0)\}$, which is the level set of energy $0$ because $\tfrac12kx^{2}+\tfrac12mv^{2}=0$ forces $x=v=0$. This is clause 4.

The rest points are the equilibria, and by [L6] the equation $U'(x)=kx=0$ has the unique solution $x=0$ because $k>0$; the origin is a strict global minimum of $U$, so [L6] gives Lyapunov stability. In that case the family of the classification is $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)$, which is exactly the motion family of the harmonic model in clause 1 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]]; hence the motions of the model with the parameter value $c=0$ are exactly those of the harmonic model with the same $m$ and $k$.

Clause 2: let $x:J\to\mathbb R$ be a motion and $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$. At every interior point $t$ of $J$, $x$ is twice differentiable and $x'$ is differentiable, so by [L3] $$e'(t)=m\,x'(t)x''(t)+k\,x(t)x'(t)=x'(t)\bigl(m\,x''(t)+k\,x(t)\bigr)=-c\,x'(t)^{2},$$ where the equation of motion was used in the last step. This is nonpositive, and it is strictly negative whenever $c>0$ and $x'(t)\neq0$.

For $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ the function $e$ is continuous on $[t_{1},t_{2}]$ and differentiable on $(t_{1},t_{2})$ with continuous derivative by step 1.2, so [L4] gives $$e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}e'(s)\,ds=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0,$$ the inequality by the pointwise nonnegativity of the integrand and the monotonicity of the integral in [L4]. Hence $e$ is nonincreasing on $J$.

Let $c>0$.
